query: Consider the following context: High entropy alloys have excellent wear resistance, so they have great application prospects in the fields of wear resistance and surface protection. In that context, which material can be used for adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A thin, high entropy alloy (HEA) coating based on an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn system will adhere effectively to a Cu matrix and improve its wear resistance under typical service conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A copper matrix exhibiting relatively low hardness and wear resistance.
generation.intervention: Deposition of a nanostructured CoCrFeNiMn HEA coating (via techniques such as magnetron sputtering) onto the Cu surface.
generation.conditions: Ambient to moderately elevated temperatures under standard wear or friction conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A nanostructured interface with enhanced interfacial bonding, where fine precipitates or nanoscale features (e.g., nanotwins) promote mechanical interlocking between the HEA and Cu substrate.
generation.mechanism: The chemical complexity of the CoCrFeNiMn HEA favors atomic intermixing at the interface, reducing lattice disregistry and creating strong metallurgical bonds. This interfacial mixing, along with the high intrinsic strength and refined microstructure of the HEA, improves load transfer and resists wear-induced cracking.
generation.predicted_outcome: The HEA-coated Cu will display improved adhesion at the interface and significantly enhanced wear resistance compared to uncoated copper, with a lower wear rate and reduced crack propagation under cyclic loading.
generation.baseline: Uncoated copper, which typically suffers from lower resistance to wear and surface degradation under applied mechanical loads.
generation.boundary: The performance of the HEA coating may be adversely affected if the thermal expansion mismatch between Cu and the HEA leads to interfacial stresses under extreme temperature conditions; the benefit might also be reduced if the deposition process does not yield a defect‐free, continuous interlayer.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative strength of the interfacial bonding and the long-term stability under cyclic thermal and mechanical loading remain to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Cu samples; deposit an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn HEA coating on one set using magnetron sputtering while leaving the other set uncoated. Subject both sets to standardized wear tests (e.g., pin-on-disk or scratch testing) and thermal cycling.
measurements: Interfacial adhesion strength (via scratch test or nanoindentation)
Microstructural characterization of the interface (using TEM/SEM) before and after wear testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA-coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in interfacial adhesion and wear resistance compared to the uncoated Cu, or if the HEA/Cu interface fails prematurely (evidenced by delamination or crack propagation localized at the interface), the hypothesis is falsified.

Question: How can high-throughput computational screening be used to discover lightweight, precipitation-strengthened high-entropy alloys with high-temperature strength superior to traditional ferritic superalloys?. System: Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary system (specifically Al20Cr5Fe50Mn20Ti5 and Al15Cr5Fe50Mn25Ti5 as successful cases). Processing: Arc-melting of 99.9 wt% purity constituent elements, melted at least six times for homogeneity, followed by drop-casting; subsequent homogenization at 1200 °C and annealing at 700 °C for 2 hours for specific characterizations. Test conditions: Compression tests at room temperature and elevated temperatures (up to 700 °C) at a strain rate of 2 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹; in situ neutron scattering from room temperature to 1050 °C; synchrotron XRD and TEM characterization.
